opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the core problem we're trying to solve is that if you just look at the neurons inside a model, they're really hard to interpret. A single neuron will fire for a bunch of unrelated things. It might respond to some piece of code, and to a mention of a sports team, and to something in French. That's polysemanticity, and it means the model's native basis isn't a great unit of analysis if you want to understand what it's doing.

So the first step, which a lot of people have worked on, is to learn a replacement representation, using something like a sparse autoencoder. You take the activations at some layer and decompose them into a much larger set of features that are sparse and, hopefully, each mean one thing. That gets you nicer building blocks, but it mostly tells you what's represented at a given point. It doesn't tell you how the model got from one representation to the next.

The cross-layer transcoder is our attempt to get at the computation itself. Instead of reconstructing activations at one layer, a transcoder learns to replace the MLP: it reads from the residual stream and predicts the MLP's output, going through a sparse layer of interpretable features. The "cross-layer" part means a feature that reads in at one layer can write out to all the layers after it. That matters because models seem to spread one conceptual computation across several layers. If you force every feature to live in a single layer, you end up with lots of near-duplicate features doing the same thing at different depths, and your graphs get really messy. Letting features span layers collapses a lot of that redundancy.

What that buys you is a replacement model. You swap the MLPs for the transcoder and get something that approximately reproduces the original model's behavior, but where the intermediate steps are made of features you can actually read. Then for a specific prompt you can build what we call an attribution graph, tracing which features caused which other features, all the way from the input tokens to the output. Because the interactions between features are roughly linear once you freeze things like attention patterns for that prompt, you can trace those paths pretty cleanly.

And that's where it gets fun, because you start seeing real mechanisms. For a question that needs two hops of reasoning, you can see the model represent the intermediate fact internally before it gets to the answer. Or with poetry, you can see it planning a rhyme word ahead of time, before it writes the line that ends with it. Those are hypotheses you can then test by intervening: turn a feature off or inject a different one, and check that the model's behavior changes the way the graph predicts.

I want to be honest about the limits, though. The replacement isn't perfect. There's always reconstruction error, which we keep as error nodes in the graph, so there are parts of the computation we're just not explaining. We're also mostly not explaining attention, the QK side of why the model attends where it does. And building these graphs and interpreting them still takes a lot of human effort. So I think of the cross-layer transcoder less as a final answer and more as a microscope. It's the best lens we've found so far for looking at a real production model and asking, step by step, what did it actually do here? It already shows us things we couldn't see before, and it's pretty clear where the lens needs to get sharper.

r001.rationale: The response says cross-layer features reduce near-duplicate representations, but does not say that maintaining a concept across layers requires repeatedly reinforcing it.

r002.rationale: It says cross-layer features collapse redundancy from similar features at different depths, but does not clearly state that repeated representations are consolidated into a single feature in the interpretation graph.

r003.rationale: The response presents the transcoder as a useful microscope, but does not state that it is nonessential to the underlying interpretability method.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the core problem we're trying to solve is that the raw units of a neural network, the neurons, don't really mean anything on their own. They're polysemantic. A single neuron fires for a bunch of unrelated things, and the concepts the model actually uses are smeared across many neurons. So if you want to understand what the model is computing, you first need a better set of variables to describe it with.

That's what the transcoder gives us. You train a replacement for the MLP layers that reconstructs their outputs, but you force it to do so through a sparse dictionary of features. And those features tend to be far more interpretable than neurons. You get a feature that's about "Texas," or a feature that's about "this is a word that rhymes with rabbit," or "the subject of this clause is a person."

The cross-layer part is important for a subtle reason. In a transformer, a concept often doesn't live cleanly in one layer. The model will start computing something at layer five and finish it at layer twelve, and the residual stream carries it along the whole way. If you train a separate dictionary at each layer, you end up with the same concept represented as a slightly different feature at every layer, and your diagram of the computation gets cluttered with these redundant chains of "feature A at layer five writes to feature A-prime at layer six" and so on. By letting a feature read from one layer and write to all subsequent layers, you collapse that. One feature can represent a concept for the whole stretch of the network where it's active. And that makes the resulting graphs dramatically simpler.

And really, the graph is the point. The transcoder isn't the end goal. The goal is to take a specific prompt, see which features turned on, and then trace how those features caused each other and ultimately caused the output. That's what we call an attribution graph. What the transcoder buys you is that the nodes in that graph are things a human can label and reason about. So when we look at how Claude does a two-digit addition, or plans a rhyme ahead of time in a poem, or decides whether it recognizes a name before it decides whether to answer, we can actually read off a mechanism rather than just a wall of numbers.

I'd also say there's an honesty check built in. Because the transcoder is a replacement model, you can measure how faithful it is. You can swap it in and see how much of the original behavior you recover. And you can perturb the features and see if the model's output changes the way the graph predicts. That matters because interpretability has a long history of producing compelling stories that turn out to be wrong. The transcoder approach gives you a way to validate the story with interventions.

It's not perfect. There's reconstruction error we have to account for, and a lot of what a model does goes through attention, which the transcoder doesn't directly explain. But as a tool for turning a model's computation into something you can actually look at, it's been the biggest step forward I've seen.

r001.rationale: The response says a concept can begin at one layer and continue to later layers via the residual stream, but does not state that maintaining it requires repeatedly reinforcing it.

r002.rationale: It explains that separate layer dictionaries create redundant representations of the same concept, while a cross-layer feature can represent that concept across its active stretch and simplify the graph.

r003.rationale: Calling the transcoder a tool rather than the end goal does not establish that it is nonessential to the underlying interpretability method.

astra-6.text:
The value is that it gives us a more interpretable approximation of the model’s computation. In a transformer, information is represented across many neurons, and an individual neuron can participate in many different concepts. So just looking at neuron activations doesn’t necessarily tell you what the model is doing.

A cross-layer transcoder tries to express that computation in terms of sparse, more interpretable features, while capturing connections across layers. That lets us move from “this feature is active” to “this feature contributed to that feature, which then contributed to the output.” We can start tracing a circuit that explains a particular behavior.

And that gives us something we can test. If we think a feature is playing a particular role, we can intervene and see whether the model’s behavior changes as predicted. The caveat is that we’re working with an approximation: it can miss computation, and a plausible-looking graph isn’t automatically a faithful explanation. But it gives us a much more useful starting point for investigating how the model arrives at an answer.

r001.rationale: The response discusses features and connections across layers, but does not say that maintaining a concept across layers requires repeatedly reinforcing it.

r002.rationale: It describes sparse features and cross-layer connections, but does not state that repeated representations of the same concept are consolidated into one graph feature.

r003.rationale: The response presents the transcoder as useful, but does not say it is optional or nonessential to the underlying interpretability method.

sol-6.1.text:
The value is that it lets us follow a computation across layers, rather than interpreting each layer in isolation. A feature might be built up using information from several earlier layers, and a cross-layer transcoder gives us a way to represent those connections in terms of more interpretable features.

So we can start to ask, “What contributed to this feature, and how did it contribute to the model’s answer?” That gets us closer to a circuit-level explanation of what the model is doing. It’s still an approximation, so we need to test those explanations with interventions, but it gives us a much more useful starting point for understanding the computation.

r001.rationale: It describes information from earlier layers contributing to a feature, but does not say that maintaining a concept across layers requires repeatedly reinforcing it.

r002.rationale: It says the transcoder represents connections using interpretable features, but does not state that repeated representations are consolidated into one feature in an interpretation graph.

r003.rationale: It does not say whether the cross-layer transcoder is essential to the underlying interpretability method.
